knowledge_statements.title: PSD–SOS Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical gap between globally nonnegative polynomials and sums of polynomial squares.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The Motzkin polynomial \(M(x,y)=x^4y^2+x^2y^4-3x^2y^2+1\) satisfies \(M(x,y)\ge0\) for every \((x,y)\in\mathbb R^2\), but there do not exist polynomials \(q_1,\ldots,q_r\in\mathbb R[x,y]\) such that \(M=\sum_{j=1}^r q_j^2\). Hence membership in the cone of globally positive-semidefinite polynomials is strictly weaker than membership in the sum-of-squares cone, even though every sum of squares is globally nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Motzkin polynomial is nonnegative everywhere but is not a sum of polynomial squares, so PSD and SOS polynomial cones differ.
assumptions_latex: Positive semidefinite means globally nonnegative on \(\mathbb R^2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\ge0\text{ on }\mathbb R^2\quad\text{and}\quad M\notin\Sigma\mathbb R[x,y]^2.\)

notation.meaning: cone of finite sums of squares in the polynomial ring

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Motzkin example is the appropriate counterexample for the PSD–SOS gap and is stated precisely, but the non-SOS assertion has no cited source or locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Strict-Positivity versus Nonnegativity Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Boundary at which strict-positivity Positivstellensätze cease to apply directly.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and compact and let \(f\in\mathbb R[x]\). If \(f>0\) on \(K\), then continuity gives a margin \(\delta=\min_{x\in K}f(x)>0\). If merely \(f\ge0\) and \(f\) vanishes somewhere on \(K\), no positive uniform margin exists. Consequently, a representation theorem whose hypothesis is strict positivity cannot be applied to \(f\) itself solely from nonnegativity; it applies to \(f+\varepsilon\) for every \(\varepsilon>0\) when its other hypotheses hold, without implying membership of \(f\) in the certificate cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict positivity on a compact set supplies a positive margin. A nonnegative polynomial with zeros lacks that margin, so strict-positivity certificates need not pass to the limit.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f>0\text{ on }K\implies\min_K f>0\), whereas \(f\ge0\) with a zero gives \(\min_K f=0\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-degree coefficient-space characterization of the strict-versus-nonstrict boundary on a compact set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be nonempty and compact, let \(V\subseteq\mathbb R[x]\) be finite-dimensional with \(1\in V\), and define \(P_V(K)=\{f\in V:f(x)\geq0\ \forall x\in K\}\). Then \[\operatorname{int}_V P_V(K)=\{f\in V:f(x)>0\ \forall x\in K\}.\] Hence a nonnegative \(f\in V\) having a zero on \(K\) lies on the boundary of \(P_V(K)\), while \(f+\varepsilon\in\operatorname{int}_V P_V(K)\) for every \(\varepsilon>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a finite-dimensional polynomial space containing constants, strict positivity on a compact set is exactly interior membership in the nonnegativity cone; a nonnegative polynomial with a zero is a boundary point.
knowledge_statements.title: Strict Positivity as Cone Interior
Polynomial versus Rational Certificate Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Field-of-functions gap between polynomial SOS certificates and denominator-assisted rational certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a globally nonnegative polynomial \(f\in\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), a polynomial-versus-rational certificate gap occurs when \(f\notin\Sigma\mathbb R[x]^2\) but there is a nonzero polynomial \(q\in\mathbb R[x]\) such that \(q^2f\in\Sigma\mathbb R[x]^2\). Equivalently, \(f\) is a sum of squares of rational functions, \(f=\sum_j(p_j/q)^2\), while it is not a sum of squares of polynomials. The denominator certificate establishes \(f(x)\ge0\) wherever \(q(x)\ne0\), and polynomial continuity extends this inequality to all points.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The gap occurs when a nonnegative polynomial is not polynomial-SOS but becomes SOS after multiplication by a squared nonzero denominator.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\notin\Sigma\mathbb R[x]^2\ \land\ q^2f\in\Sigma\mathbb R[x]^2\) defines the gap.

notation.meaning: cone of finite sums of polynomial squares

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly distinguishes polynomial SOS from rational-function SOS using a common squared denominator, but the equivalence and denominator-assisted certificate claim lack a source with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Strict Gram Feasibility Forces Rational Descent
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A coefficient-field SOS gap cannot occur when the rational Gram affine space contains a positive-definite real point.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in\mathbb Q[x]\), let \(v\) be a monomial vector with rational entries, and set \(\mathcal A_f=\{Q\in\mathbb S^N:v^TQv=f\}\). If \(\mathcal A_f\cap\mathbb S_{++}^N\neq\varnothing\), then \(\mathcal A_f\) contains a positive-definite rational matrix. Consequently, \(f\) is a sum of squares of polynomials in \(\mathbb Q[x]\). Thus a real SOS representation that does not descend to \(\mathbb Q\) requires every feasible real Gram matrix to be singular.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Strict real Gram feasibility guarantees a rational positive-definite Gram matrix, so a genuine coefficient-field gap requires boundary-only Gram feasibility.
assumptions_latex: \(f\in\mathbb Q[x]\) and the chosen Gram basis is rational.
The coefficient-matching affine space contains a real positive-definite matrix.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal A_f\cap\mathbb S_{++}^N\neq\varnothing\Rightarrow f\in\Sigma\mathbb Q[x]^2\).

notation.meaning: rational affine space of coefficient-matching Gram matrices

knowledge_statements.title: Strict Gram Feasibility Forces Rational Descent

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient boundary-face condition for descent of a real Gram certificate to rational coefficients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in\mathbb Q[x]\), let \(v\in\mathbb Q[x]^N\), and let \(Q\in\mathbb S_+^N\) satisfy \(v^{\mathsf T}Qv=f\). If \(\ker Q\) has a basis in \(\mathbb Q^N\), then the rational coefficient-matching affine space contains a rational positive-semidefinite matrix \(Q_{\mathbb Q}\) with the same kernel and \(v^{\mathsf T}Q_{\mathbb Q}v=f\). Consequently \(f\) is a sum of squares of polynomials in \(\mathbb Q[x]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A real Gram certificate whose kernel is rational descends to a rational Gram certificate even on the PSD boundary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \ker Q\text{ rational}\Longrightarrow\exists Q_{\mathbb Q}\in\mathbb S_+^N\cap\mathbb Q^{N\times N}:v^{\mathsf T}Q_{\mathbb Q}v=f.

notation.meaning: Nullspace determining the PSD face containing \(Q\).

review_flags: This is a sufficient descent criterion, not a classification of irrational boundary faces.
The conclusion concerns the chosen rational Gram template.
knowledge_statements.title: Rational-Kernel Descent Criterion
Real versus Rational Coefficient Gap
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Coefficient-field obstruction for otherwise identical algebraic certificate templates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\), let \(f,g_1,\ldots,g_m\in\mathbb Q[x]\), and fix a certificate template \(f=\sigma_0+\sum_{i=1}^m\sigma_i g_i\) with prescribed degree bounds and each \(\sigma_i\) a sum of squares. A real-versus-rational coefficient gap for this template occurs when suitable \(\sigma_i\in\Sigma\mathbb R[x]^2\) exist, but no suitable \(\tau_i\in\Sigma\mathbb Q[x]^2\) satisfy the same identity and bounds. Thus the gap concerns descent of a fixed real certificate to rational data; it is not merely failure to recover rational coefficients numerically.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The gap occurs when a fixed bounded-degree certificate exists with real coefficients but no certificate of the same form exists over the rationals.
assumptions_latex: The certificate form and degree bounds are fixed before comparing fields.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\in M_{\mathbb R,d}(g)\setminus M_{\mathbb Q,d}(g)\) defines a real-versus-rational coefficient gap.

notation.meaning: degree-bounded certificate cone generated over coefficient field F
finite sums of squares of polynomials over F

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\in\Sigma L[x]^2\Longrightarrow f\in\Sigma\mathbb Q[x]^2\).

review_flags: Needs a field-descent source verifying the rational sum-of-squares diagonalization of the positive trace form.
The statement concerns unconstrained SOS identities and does not establish descent for arbitrary bounded multiblock quadratic-module templates.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Proposed coefficient-field regime in which an algebraic SOS identity descends to rational coefficients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L/\mathbb Q\) be a finite totally real extension and let \(f\in\mathbb Q[x]\). If \(f=\sum_{i=1}^r q_i^2\) with \(q_i\in L[x]\), then \(f=[L:\mathbb Q]^{-1}\sum_i\operatorname{Tr}_{L/\mathbb Q}(q_i^2)\). The proposed conclusion is that positivity of the trace form yields a finite sum-of-squares representation in \(\mathbb Q[x]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An SOS representation over a finite totally real number field is proposed to descend to a rational SOS representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Totally Real Trace Descent for SOS Identities
knowledge_statements.title: Totally Real Trace Descent for SOS Identities

intermediate_metadata.reason: This leaf owns descent of a fixed bounded algebraic certificate template from real to rational coefficients. Accepted results cover strict feasibility and rational-kernel faces only. Rational-function representations and numerical recovery are excluded to sibling or method scopes. Without an accepted definition, a verified strict example, or a reliable general boundary obstruction theorem, the essential topic remains materially incomplete.

knowledge_statements.title: Compactness without Archimedeanity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes geometric compactness from an Archimedean property of chosen generators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For generators \(g=(g_1,\ldots,g_m)\subset\mathbb R[x]\), let \(K(g)=\{x:g_i(x)\ge0\}\) and \(M(g)=\{\sigma_0+\sum_i\sigma_i g_i:\sigma_i\in\Sigma\mathbb R[x]^2\}\). The module is Archimedean when \(N-\sum_{j=1}^n x_j^2\in M(g)\) for some \(N>0\), which implies that \(K(g)\) is compact. The converse is not automatic for an arbitrary presentation: compactness of \(K(g)\) alone does not supply the displayed algebraic membership. Therefore an Archimedean Positivstellensatz requires the module condition or an equivalent certified bounding constraint, not compactness alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An Archimedean quadratic module forces compactness, but a compact feasible set does not automatically make an arbitrary chosen generator module Archimedean.
assumptions_latex: \(M(g)\) denotes the quadratic module of the displayed generators.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M(g)\text{ Archimedean}\implies K(g)\text{ compact}\), but the converse need not hold for a fixed presentation.

notation.meaning: basic closed semialgebraic set defined by g

assumptions_latex: \(g=(g_1,\ldots,g_m)\) and \(h=(h_1,\ldots,h_s)\) are finite polynomial generator lists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M(g)\subseteq M(h)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact algebraic condition sufficient for transferring every certificate from one presentation to another.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g=(g_1,\ldots,g_m)\) and \(h=(h_1,\ldots,h_s)\). If every generator \(g_i\) belongs to \(M(h)\), then \[M(g)\subseteq M(h).\] Every quadratic-module certificate in the \(g\)-presentation can therefore be converted to an \(h\)-certificate by replacing each \(g_i\) with an \(M(h)\)-representation. Equality of feasible sets is neither required for this implication nor sufficient in place of the membership assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Certificates transfer from one presentation to another whenever every source generator belongs to the target quadratic module.
knowledge_statements.title: Generator-Wise Module Inclusion Criterion

assumptions_latex: The empty presentation is permitted and generates the SOS cone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K(g)=K(h)=\mathbb R^2\) but \(M(g)\subsetneq M(h)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit same-set, different-module example produced by a redundant globally nonnegative generator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[m(x,y)=x^4y^2+x^2y^4+1-3x^2y^2.\] The Motzkin polynomial is globally nonnegative but is not a sum of squares. Let \(g\) be the empty generator list and \(h=(m)\). Then \[K(g)=\mathbb R^2=K(h),\qquad M(g)=\Sigma\mathbb R[x,y]^2,\] while \(m\in M(h)\setminus M(g)\). Hence \(M(g)\subsetneq M(h)\) although the two presentations define the same feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adding the globally nonnegative non-SOS Motzkin polynomial as a redundant inequality leaves the feasible set unchanged but strictly enlarges the quadratic module.
knowledge_statements.statement_title: A Redundant Nonnegative Generator Strictly Enlarges the Certificate Module
knowledge_statements.title: A Redundant Nonnegative Generator Strictly Enlarges the Certificate Module
Generator-Dependent Certification
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Certificate membership can depend on the polynomial presentation of the same feasible set.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g=(g_1,\ldots,g_m)\) and \(h=(h_1,\ldots,h_s)\) satisfy \(K(g)=K(h)\), while their quadratic modules \(M(g)\) and \(M(h)\) differ. Positivity of a polynomial on the common set is presentation-independent, but the assertions \(f\in M(g)\) and \(f\in M(h)\) are algebraic membership statements in different cones. Consequently, equality of feasible sets does not by itself imply equivalence of the two certificate systems; certification transfers only when an inclusion such as \(M(g)\subseteq M(h)\) is established or the particular representation is converted explicitly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two generator lists may define the same feasible set but different quadratic modules, so certificate membership can depend on the chosen presentation.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) and \(h\) are finite polynomial generator lists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(K(g)=K(h)\not\Rightarrow M(g)=M(h)\).

notation.meaning: set defined by nonnegativity of the generators g

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement correctly separates presentation-independent positivity from generator-dependent module membership, but no cited example or authoritative locator supports the asserted possible inequality of modules defining the same set.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A feasible ray with negative leading objective coefficient certifies escape to minus infinity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose \(x_0+tu\in K\) for all \(t\geq0\), where \(u\neq0\), and \(f(x_0+tu)=\sum_{j=0}^r a_jt^j\) with \(r\geq1\) and \(a_r<0\). Then \(f(x_0+tu)\to-\infty\) as \(t\to\infty\), and hence \(\inf_{x\in K}f(x)=-\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible ray whose restricted objective has negative leading coefficient certifies unboundedness below.
assumptions_latex: \(f(x_0+tu)\) has positive degree and negative leading coefficient.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in K}f(x)=-\infty\).

notation.meaning: leading coefficient of the objective restricted to the ray

knowledge_statements.title: Feasible-Ray Certificate of Unboundedness

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary asymptotic feasibility conditions derived from the leading homogeneous parts of the chosen generators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\{x:g_i(x)\geq0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\), let \(d_i=\deg g_i\), and let \(g_i^{[d_i]}\) be the degree-\(d_i\) homogeneous part of \(g_i\). If \(x_k\in K\), \(\lVert x_k\rVert\to\infty\), and \(x_k/\lVert x_k\rVert\to u\), then \(g_i^{[d_i]}(u)\geq0\) for every \(i\). Thus emptiness of \(\{u\in S^{n-1}:g_i^{[d_i]}(u)\geq0\ \forall i\}\) implies that \(K\) is bounded; the converse need not hold.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every normalized escape direction satisfies the leading homogeneous generator inequalities, so emptiness of that directional set rules out escape, though the test is not necessary for boundedness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(g_i^{[d_i]}(u)\geq0\) for all \(i\).

notation.meaning: leading homogeneous part of the generator

knowledge_statements.title: Leading-Form Screen for Escape Directions

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Elementary closed basic-semialgebraic examples distinguish finite nonattainment at infinity from unbounded descent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K_1=\{(x,y):xy-1\geq0,\ 1-xy\geq0,\ x\geq0\}\) and \(f_1(x,y)=x\). Then \(K_1\) is closed, \(\inf_{K_1}f_1=0\), and the infimum is not attained, since \((1/k,k)\in K_1\) escapes to infinity and \(f_1(1/k,k)\to0\). By contrast, on \(K_2=\mathbb R\), \(f_2(x)=-x\) tends to \(-\infty\) along \(x\to+\infty\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One closed polynomially described set has a finite unattained infimum approached at infinity, while a second example has objective value tending to minus infinity.
assumptions_latex: The feasible sets and objectives are as displayed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{K_1}f_1=0\) is unattained, whereas \(\inf_{K_2}f_2=-\infty\).

notation.meaning: positive branch of the hyperbola xy=1

knowledge_statements.title: Canonical Escape Outcomes
Noncompact Escape Directions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sequences escaping to infinity expose the missing boundedness behind compact-set certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:g_i(x)\ge0\}\) be closed. A noncompact escape direction is witnessed by a sequence \((x_k)\subset K\) with \(\lVert x_k\rVert\to\infty\); after normalization and passage to a subsequence, \(x_k/\lVert x_k\rVert\to u\) for some \(\lVert u\rVert=1\). Along such a sequence, a polynomial objective may approach its infimum without attaining it, or may tend to \(-\infty\). Hence compactness-based positivity and convergence results cannot be invoked unless coercivity, an Archimedean certificate, or another condition excludes every feasible escape sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A feasible sequence escaping to infinity can destroy attainment or boundedness, so compact-set certificate results require an explicit mechanism excluding escape.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists x_k\in K:\lVert x_k\rVert\to\infty\), so compactness-based conclusions require an additional exclusion condition.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The escape-sequence characterization is precise under closed noncompactness and the failure-boundary kind fits the leaf, but the optimization and certificate consequences have no supporting source locator.

children.title: Singular Zero Sets
children.top_down_role: Zero loci whose singular structure affects positivity representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Singular Zero Sets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Singular points of a polynomial hypersurface where first-order geometry degenerates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(f\in\mathbb R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\), its real zero set is \(Z_{\mathbb R}(f)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:f(x)=0\}\). A point \(a\in Z_{\mathbb R}(f)\) is singular when \(\nabla f(a)=0\); otherwise it is regular. More generally, for \(Z_{\mathbb R}(f_1,\ldots,f_r)\), a point is singular relative to the expected codimension \(r\) when the Jacobian matrix \(J_f(a)\) has rank less than \(r\). At a singular zero, the usual first-order tangent-hyperplane description degenerates, which can obstruct local analyses used by positivity certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A zero of one polynomial is singular when its gradient vanishes; for several equations, singularity is detected by deficient Jacobian rank.
assumptions_latex: For multiple equations, codimension \(r\) is the local expected codimension.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(a\in Z_{\mathbb R}(f)\text{ is singular}\iff\nabla f(a)=0\).

notation.meaning: real algebraic zero set of f

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Differential Structure at a Nonnegative Zero
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary first- and second-order structure at an interior zero of a locally nonnegative polynomial.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f\in\mathbb R[x]\) be nonnegative on a neighborhood of \(a\) and satisfy \(f(a)=0\). Then \(\nabla f(a)=0\) and \(\nabla^2f(a)\succeq0\). Thus an interior zero of a locally nonnegative polynomial is a singular hypersurface zero. These differential conditions are necessary but not sufficient for local nonnegativity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An interior nonnegative zero has zero gradient and positive-semidefinite Hessian, but those conditions alone do not ensure local nonnegativity.
assumptions_latex: \(f\) is nonnegative on a neighborhood of \(a\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nabla f(a)=0\) and \(\nabla^2f(a)\succeq0\).

notation.meaning: Hessian of f at the zero

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines contact data at a boundary zero using feasible analytic arcs and active constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:g_i(x)\geq0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\), let \(x^*\in K\) satisfy \(I(x^*)\neq\varnothing\), and let \(f(x^*)=0\). For a nonconstant real-analytic arc \(\gamma:[0,\varepsilon)\to K\) with \(\gamma(0)=x^*\), its boundary-contact data are \[\bigl(\operatorname{ord}_0(f\circ\gamma),\ (\operatorname{ord}_0(g_i\circ\gamma))_{i\in I(x^*)}\bigr),\qquad I(x^*)=\{i:g_i(x^*)=0\}.\] An infinite order is assigned to an identically vanishing composition. These data describe how the objective zero and active boundary components meet along feasible directions, including contacts invisible to first-order tangent information.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Boundary contact geometry records the vanishing orders of the objective and active constraints along every feasible analytic arc through a zero with at least one active boundary constraint.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parity obstruction to nonnegativity along a two-sided feasible analytic arc.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\gamma:(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)\to\mathbb R^n\) be real analytic with \(\gamma(0)=x^*\), and suppose \(f\circ\gamma\not\equiv0\). If \(\operatorname{ord}_0(f\circ\gamma)\) is odd, then \(f\circ\gamma\) changes sign at zero. Consequently, if both sides of the arc are feasible near zero, then \(f\) is not nonnegative on the local feasible set and admits no positivity certificate sound there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Odd finite vanishing order forces a sign change along a two-sided arc and obstructs local positivity when both branches are feasible.
assumptions_latex: \(\gamma\) is a two-sided real-analytic arc whose two branches are feasible near zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\circ\gamma\) changes sign at \(0\).

notation.meaning: first nonzero Taylor order of f along the arc

Vanishing-Order Obstructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary arcwise order condition for certificates whose summands remain nonnegative near a zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a proposed local certificate has \(f=\sum_{j=0}^s \sigma_j h_j\), where every \(\sigma_j\) is a sum of squares and every \(h_j\circ\gamma\) is nonnegative near zero for a feasible real-analytic arc \(\gamma\) through \(x^*\). If \(f\circ\gamma\not\equiv0\), then \[\operatorname{ord}_0(f\circ\gamma)=\min_{j:\,\sigma_jh_j\circ\gamma\not\equiv0}\operatorname{ord}_0((\sigma_jh_j)\circ\gamma).\] Moreover, each finite \(\operatorname{ord}_0(\sigma_j\circ\gamma)\) is even. Failure of these order constraints rules out the proposed certificate structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Along a feasible analytic arc, nonnegative certificate summands cannot cancel their lowest-order terms; SOS factors also vanish to even order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{ord}_0(f\circ\gamma)=\min_j\operatorname{ord}_0((\sigma_jh_j)\circ\gamma)\), over nonzero summands, and finite SOS-factor orders are even.

If \(f\in M(g)\), then the germ \(f_{x^*}\) belongs to the quadratic module generated by the germs \((g_i)_{x^*}\) in the local ring at \(x^*\). Consequently, \(f_{x^*}\notin M_{x^*}(g)\) implies \(f\notin M(g)\).

Local Positivity Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local negativity near a candidate zero precludes any sound positivity certificate on the neighborhood.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(x^*\in K\), and let \(M\subseteq\mathbb R[x]\) be a certificate cone satisfying \(p(x)\geq0\) for every \(p\in M\) and every \(x\in K\cap U\), where \(U\) is a neighborhood of \(x^*\). If there exists a sequence \(x_k\in K\cap U\) with \(x_k\to x^*\) and \(f(x_k)<0\), then \(f\notin M\). Thus a single feasible negative branch accumulating at \(x^*\) is a local obstruction to any certificate cone that is sound on \(K\cap U\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If feasible points with negative objective values accumulate at a candidate zero, no locally sound positivity cone can certify that polynomial.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates strict-positivity membership from saturation by all nonnegative polynomials.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Saturation of \(Q(g)\) means \(Q(g)=\operatorname{Pos}(K(g))\) and therefore requires membership of every nonnegative polynomial, including polynomials vanishing on \(K(g)\). Consequently, a quadratic module may certify every strictly positive polynomial while remaining nonsaturated because some nonnegative polynomial with a zero on \(K(g)\) is absent.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists d_*<\infty:\ f\in Q_d(g)\iff d\geq d_*\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Monotone threshold structure for a certificate that exists in the full module.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For nested exhaustive truncations \(Q_0(g)\subseteq Q_1(g)\subseteq\cdots\), if \(f\in Q(g)=\bigcup_{d\geq0}Q_d(g)\), then \[d_*(f;g)=\min\{d:f\in Q_d(g)\}<\infty.\] Consequently, \(f\notin Q_d(g)\) for \(d<d_*\) and \(f\in Q_d(g)\) for every \(d\geq d_*\). Thus this pathology is transient as the cutoff increases, unlike absence of finite detection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A certificate in the full module has a least detecting order; lower truncations miss it and every truncation at or above that order contains it.
knowledge_statements.title: Minimal Detecting Truncation

assumptions_latex: The truncation bounds every product \(\sigma_i g_i\) by degree \(2d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f\in Q(g)\setminus Q_d(g)\) means that every valid certificate exceeds truncation order \(d\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A valid quadratic-module certificate may require degree exceeding the relaxation cutoff.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For generators \(g_0=1,g_1,\ldots,g_m\), define the order-\(d\) truncation \[Q_d(g)=\left\{\sum_{i=0}^m\sigma_i g_i:\ \sigma_i\in\Sigma[x],\ \deg(\sigma_i g_i)\leq2d\right\}.\] A polynomial \(f\) has certificate degree beyond truncation \(d\) precisely when \(f\in Q(g)=\bigcup_{r\geq0}Q_r(g)\) but \(f\notin Q_d(g)\). Consequently, failure of the order-\(d\) semidefinite feasibility problem does not refute membership in the full quadratic module; it only refutes a certificate satisfying the imposed degree bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A certificate lies beyond truncation when it exists in the full quadratic module but no representation satisfies the current degree cutoff.
knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Degree beyond the Truncation

assumptions_latex: \(Q_d(g)\) is viewed in its finite-dimensional coefficient space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dist}(p,Q_d(g))=0\) although \(p\notin Q_d(g)\), and no continuous linear functional strictly separates \(p\) from \(Q_d(g)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimization and separation consequences of a nonclosed truncated certificate image.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(p\in\overline{Q_d(g)}\setminus Q_d(g)\) in a finite-dimensional coefficient norm, then \[\operatorname{dist}(p,Q_d(g))=0\quad\text{but}\quad p\notin Q_d(g).\] Hence minimizing coefficient residual over truncated certificates has infimum zero without an exact zero-residual certificate. Moreover, no continuous linear functional can strictly separate \(p\) from \(Q_d(g)\), because every continuous functional nonnegative on \(Q_d(g)\) is also nonnegative on its closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At a nonclosed-image limit, the best coefficient residual is zero although no exact certificate exists, and continuous linear separation cannot distinguish the limit from the cone.
knowledge_statements.title: Zero Distance Without Exact Membership

knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-variable fixed-order witness whose certificate polynomials converge outside the image.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g(x)=-x^2\) and \(Q_1(g)=\{\sigma_0+\sigma_1g:\sigma_0\in\Sigma\mathbb R[x]^2,\ \deg\sigma_0\le2,\ \sigma_1\in\mathbb R_+\}\). For \(k\ge1\), set \(\sigma_{0,k}(x)=k^{-1}+x+(k/4)x^2=(k^{-1/2}+(\sqrt{k}/2)x)^2\) and \(\sigma_{1,k}=k/4\). Then \(p_k=\sigma_{0,k}-\sigma_{1,k}x^2=k^{-1}+x\in Q_1(g)\) and \(p_k\to x\). Yet \(x\notin Q_1(g)\): writing \(x=a+2bx+(c-s)x^2\) with \(\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\b&c\end{pmatrix}\succeq0\) and \(s\ge0\) forces \(a=0\), hence \(b=0\), contradicting \(2b=1\). Thus \(Q_1(g)\) is not closed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At fixed order, certificates for one over k plus x converge to x, but x itself has no certificate in the truncated quadratic module.
assumptions_latex: The truncation permits a quadratic SOS free term and a nonnegative constant multiplier of \(g\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: p_k=k^{-1}+x\in Q_1(g),\quad p_k\to x,\quad x\notin Q_1(g).

Nonclosed Truncated Images
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonclosed coefficient images can create unattained limits of bounded-degree SOS representations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix \(d\), choose monomial vectors \(v_i\), and let \[\mathcal L_d((Q_i)_{i=0}^m)=\sum_{i=0}^m g_i v_i^{\mathsf T}Q_i v_i,\qquad Q_i\succeq0,\] with degrees chosen so every term has degree at most \(2d\). The truncated image is nonclosed when there are feasible tuples \((Q_i^{(k)})\) whose coefficient polynomials \(p_k=\mathcal L_d((Q_i^{(k)}))\) converge to \(p\), while no positive-semidefinite tuple maps exactly to \(p\). Then \(p\in\overline{Q_d(g)}\setminus Q_d(g)\), so arbitrarily small coefficient residuals need not yield an exact truncated certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A truncated SOS image is nonclosed when certifiable coefficient vectors converge to a limit having no feasible Gram representation.
assumptions_latex: The Gram-vector degrees are fixed at truncation order \(d\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(K=\{x:g_i(x)\geq0,\ i=1,\ldots,m\}\), and suppose the quadratic module \(Q(g)\) is Archimedean. If \(f>0\) on \(K\), Putinar's Positivstellensatz gives \(f\in Q(g)\). Because every polynomial identity in \(Q(g)\) has finite degree, \(f\in Q_d(g)\) for some finite \(d\). Thus absence of finite detection is impossible under these two hypotheses; failure of either hypothesis does not by itself imply nondetection.

Ill-Conditioned Polynomial Bases
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quantifies how polynomial basis changes amplify coefficient and Gram-matrix conditioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v(x)\) be a polynomial basis vector and let \(w(x)=T v(x)\) for an invertible matrix \(T\). If \(p(x)=v(x)^{\mathsf T}Qv(x)=w(x)^{\mathsf T}Rw(x)\), then \[R=T^{-\mathsf T}QT^{-1}.\] Hence perturbations in Gram coordinates can be amplified by factors controlled by \(\lVert T^{-1}\rVert^2\), while conversion back to the original coordinates is controlled by \(\lVert T\rVert^2\). A large condition number \(\kappa(T)\) therefore makes coefficient matching and positive-semidefiniteness tests sensitive to rounding, even though exact SOS representability is basis invariant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: SOS representability is basis invariant, but an ill-conditioned basis transformation can strongly amplify Gram and coefficient errors.
assumptions_latex: \(w=Tv\) and both vectors span the same polynomial space.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R=T^{-\mathsf T}QT^{-1}\), with perturbation amplification governed quadratically by the conditioning of \(T\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient PSD validation test for an exact Gram matrix enclosed around a numerical approximation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\in\mathbb S^N\) be an exact coefficient-matched Gram matrix, let \(\|Q-\widehat Q\|_2\leq\eta\) be a rigorous enclosure, and let \(\underline\lambda\leq\lambda_{\min}(\widehat Q)\) be rigorously certified. Then \[\lambda_{\min}(Q)\geq\underline\lambda-\eta.\] Thus \(\underline\lambda\geq\eta\) certifies \(Q\succeq0\), and \(\underline\lambda>\eta\) certifies \(Q\succ0\). If \(\underline\lambda<\eta\), this test is inconclusive rather than evidence that \(Q\) is indefinite.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rigorous matrix enclosure certifies PSD when a rigorous lower bound on the computed minimum eigenvalue dominates the enclosure error; otherwise the test is inconclusive.

knowledge_statements.title: Eigenvalue-Margin Validation from a Rigorous Gram Enclosure
Near-Boundary Gram Matrices
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Small eigenvalue margins make numerical Gram positivity nonrobust.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Q\succeq0\) be a Gram matrix for an SOS polynomial and set \(\delta=\lambda_{\min}(Q)\). For any symmetric perturbation \(E\), \[\lambda_{\min}(Q+E)\geq\delta-\lVert E\rVert_2.\] Thus positive semidefiniteness is guaranteed under perturbation only when \(\lVert E\rVert_2\leq\delta\). If \(\delta\) is zero or comparable to numerical error, an arbitrarily small or tolerance-sized perturbation can move the computed matrix outside the positive-semidefinite cone. A solver-reported near-boundary Gram matrix therefore lacks a robust positivity margin and requires exact or interval validation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When a Gram matrix has a tiny minimum eigenvalue, rounding of comparable size can destroy positive semidefiniteness and invalidate the SOS certificate.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lambda_{\min}(Q+E)\geq\delta-\lVert E\rVert_2\); robustness requires perturbations no larger than the spectral margin.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose floating-point computation returns positive-semidefinite matrices \(\widehat Q_i\) and the polynomial \[\widehat p=\sum_{i=0}^m g_i v_i^{\mathsf T}\widehat Q_i v_i.\] Define the identity residual \(r=f-\widehat p\). If a rigorous bound \(\lvert r(x)\rvert\leq\varepsilon\) holds on \(K\), then only \(f(x)\geq-\varepsilon\) follows from \(\widehat p(x)\geq0\). Exact nonnegativity of \(f\) requires eliminating the residual or separately proving a correction that absorbs it.
